title: Predicting Breast Cancer Treatment Response from Biopsy Slides
text:
Problem
Can H&E biopsy whole-slide images help predict pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant (pre-surgery) therapy in breast cancer patients?

title: Predicting Breast Cancer Treatment Response from Biopsy Slides
text:
Approach

Data: whole-slide images from ~100 patients, accessed in a secure environment
Preprocessing: tissue detection and tiling of whole-slide images
Feature extraction: tile embeddings from Phikon, a pathology foundation model
Modeling: PCA-reduced embeddings combined with clinical data (including cancer subtype) in a logistic regression model

title: Predicting Breast Cancer Treatment Response from Biopsy Slides
text:
My role
I focused on whole-slide image processing and foundation-model embedding extraction, building one of the two pipelines the team developed in parallel.

Image features alone carried some signal (ROC-AUC 0.70), and adding them to cancer subtype gave the best model (0.882 vs. 0.858 for subtype alone). With roughly 100 patients, these differences are small enough that they would need validation on a larger patient sample. Models were assessed wit 5-fold cross validation on a training set with final performance reported on a held-out test set.

title: Predicting Breast Cancer Treatment Response from Biopsy Slides
2nd place at UBC in National Health Datathon
text:
Original LinkedIn post
This past weekend my team placed 2nd at UBC in the National Health Datathon 2026 led by UofT’s Temerty Centre for AI Research and Education in Medicine (T-CAIREM). I really enjoyed working with a group of talented individuals from across health and data-related disciplines.
Our work explored whether biopsy slides can help predict how breast cancer patients respond to pre-surgery therapy. Working with whole-slide images from about 100 patients, we preprocessed the images and extracted embeddings using Phikon, a pathology foundation model. We then reduced those feature embeddings using PCA and combined them with cancer subtype in a logistic regression model to predict pathological complete response. In our experiments, adding image features improved on a baseline that used cancer subtype alone.
My own focus was on whole-slide image processing and extracting embeddings from the foundation model, where I built one of the two pipelines our team developed in parallel. I was impressed with how much a pretrained foundation model let us do with so little data.
The work was done on confidential clinical data in a secure environment so the data and code unfortunately can’t be shared.
A big thank you to UBC Data Science and Health (DASH) for hosting the UBC site and to my teammates Vincent Luong, Joseph Lenczowski, April Lee, Daegan Sit, and Muse Park.
I look forward to participating in more events like this in the future!

title: End-to-end Expected Goals (xG) NHL Model
text:
Link to deployed app: https://xg-web-app.onrender.com
The app may take a minute to wake up, this is expected.
Link to github repository: https://github.com/grahamgreene88/Expected-Goals-xG-Model
This project is an end-to-end machine learning application. The three main components of the project are:

Data pipelines that ingest play-by-play data daily from the NHL API and store in an Aiven cloud postgres database
An XGBoost ML xG model that was trained shot data from 2019-20 through 2024-25 and evaluted on the 2025-26 holdout test
Streamlit web app with shot explorer and team-level xG trends deployed to Render web service

For more detailed information, please visit the README file in the github repository linked above.



xGF% Chart from the Team xG Trends page of the deployed web app.

title: About
text: I grew up in Ottawa and lived two years abroad in Paris during my early teens. I completed my undegraduate degree in Chemical Engineering at Queen’s Uinversity with a specialization in Biochemical Engineering. After a bioprocess research internship in Montreal, and data science research in my 4th year to predict antibiotic resistance using gene sequence data, I decided I wanted to apply data science to bioprocess engineering. This led me to working as a Process Data Scientist with Sanofi for their vaccine manufacturing operations in Toronto. In this role I performed multivariate analysis to support root-cause investigations, built interactive applications to provide useful predictions and analytics and worked with production data pipelines to bring manufacturing data to users.

title: About
text:
Why Data Science
I am passionate about using data to build solutions to address one of the world’s greatest challenges - human health. I really enjoy diving deep into data to uncover hidden relationships and trends that can then be leveraged to make useful predictions. I want to take advantage of the growing amount of data in healthcare-related fields to create innovative solutions to improve human health.
